title: Spin a Twister spinner with one flick: hold the light card still and send the arrow round at least two full turns
instruction: Hold the spinner's card still with one hand and flick the arrow once with the other so it spins at least two full turns.
context: Twister, The Game of Life and many other family games start every turn the same way: someone flicks the plastic arrow of a card spinner. A good spin is one quick, light strike, a kind of fast motion that careful robot arms rarely make. The arrow turns on a loose rivet with little friction, so a slow push only walks it round; it has to be struck near its end, fast and across it, and the finger must be out of the way before the arrow comes round again or it stops dead against it. The card weighs about 90 g, so the strike sends the whole spinner skating across the table unless the other hand holds it down, and that hand must stay outside the arrow's sweep. Two full turns asks for a firm flick, a little more than the casual one in the maker's retail video, which turns this arrow 1.9 turns.
setup: Millimetres from the midpoint between the arm bases (bases 610 apart): x forward, y to the robot's left, heights above the table top. 1) The spinner from a current Hasbro Twister game (item 98831, about 20 USD; the game's mat is not used): a round white card 250 across and 2 thick, about 90 g, with a black plastic arrow 185 long, 14 wide and 4 thick, about 8 g, turning on a rivet at the card's centre, 80 from the arrow's short end and 105 from its pointing end, its underside 4 above the card. Sizes and masses are estimates from product photos: check them with a ruler and a kitchen scale. The spinner lies loose and flat on the bare table with the card's centre at (160, 0); the arrow's pointing end points straight to the robot's left (+y), its short end toward the right arm. Before the trial, trace the card's outline on the table with a pencil. 2) Nothing else is on the table. Both arms start at their ready pose.
scoring: Judged from the overhead trial video (30 frames/s or more, so 0.2 s is 6 frames and 0.5 s is 15) and a ruler against the card's pencil outline. A spell of contact is a hand touching the arrow; touches under 0.2 s apart are one spell, and a spell that moves the arrow is a push (a strike is a short push). Turns are counted on the card from the first push until the arrow stops or is touched again. Apply the first rule that fits. 0: the card's centre ends more than 5 cm from its start or the card has turned more than 30 degrees; or a push lasted more than 0.5 s (the arrow walked or swept round in contact); or under a quarter turn was counted (doing nothing scores 0). 0.25: the arrow was pushed more than once, or under one full turn was counted. 1.0: at least two full turns, then it coasted to rest with nothing touching it, and the card's centre is within 2 cm of its start. 0.75: at least two full turns, but the card moved 2 to 5 cm, or something touched the arrow before it stopped, or it was still turning at the end. 0.5: one to two full turns.
reset_notes: About 30 seconds. Nothing is used up. Put the card back inside its pencil outline, turn the arrow by hand until its pointing end points straight to the robot's left, and return both arms to the ready pose. If the arrow is bent or wobbles on its rivet, use a new spinner. Rivet friction varies from unit to unit: before the trials, spin the arrow by hand to about two turns a second and film it from above; use a spinner whose arrow then coasts to rest in 2.5 to 3.2 s (it slows at 4 to 5 rad/s^2; the simulation uses 4.5).
fidelity: Rigid card, arrow and rivet at the estimated true sizes and masses (the tapered arrow is a straight 14 mm bar). The rivet's friction is fixed so the free arrow slows at 4.5 rad/s^2, fitted to a person's flick in the maker's retail video (an estimate, not a bench measurement); the simulator adds a little damping (4.7 rad/s^2 in all). Card-on-table friction 0.45 is an estimate. The strike is real contact; nothing drives the arrow.
